summary.text: Modulo \(p=2m+1\), Lucas-type binomial congruences pair the terms indexed by \(k\) and \(p+k\) to show both sums vanish at every \(p+s\) with \(0\le s<p\); at \(p-1\), \(\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\) gives the first anti-diagonal value \(1\), while divisibility of central binomial coefficients leaves only \(k=m\) in the second sum, giving \((-1)^m\). Thus each Hankel matrix is anti-triangular modulo \(p\); reversing the order contributes sign \((-1)^m\), so the determinants are respectively \((-1)^m\) and \((-1)^m((-1)^m)^p=1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
             \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
We prove that, for every odd prime \(p\),
\[
\det(a(i+j))_{0\leq i,j<p}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p
\]
and
\[
\det(c(i+j))_{0\leq i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]

Write
\[
p=2m+1,
\qquad m=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
All congruences below are modulo \(p\).

We first record the binomial congruences that will be used. The one-digit form of Lucas's theorem says that if
\[
N=pq+r,\qquad K=pu+t,\qquad 0\le r,t<p,
\]
then
\[
\binom NK\equiv \binom qu\binom rt\pmod p.
\tag{1}
\]
For completeness, this follows by comparing the coefficient of \(X^K\) in
\[
(1+X)^N=(1+X)^{pq+r}\equiv (1+X^p)^q(1+X)^r\pmod p,
\]
where the congruence uses \((1+X)^p\equiv1+X^p\pmod p\). Since \(r<p\), the coefficient in question is exactly the product in (1).

Fix an integer \(s\) with \(0\le s<p\). Applying (1) to \(p+s\) gives, whenever \(0\le k\le s\),
\[
\binom{p+s}{k}\equiv\binom{s}{k},
\qquad
\binom{p+s}{p+k}\equiv\binom{s}{k}.
\tag{2}
\]
On the other hand, if \(s<k<p\), then
\[
\binom{p+s}{k}\equiv\binom{s}{k}=0.
\tag{3}
\]

We will also need a congruence for central binomial coefficients. Put
\[
D_r=\binom{2r}{r}.
\]
For every \(0\le r<p\),
\[
D_{p+r}\equiv 2D_r.
\tag{4}
\]
Indeed, first suppose \(2r<p\). The base-\(p\) decompositions of the upper and lower arguments of \(D_{p+r}\) are
\[
2(p+r)=2p+2r,
\qquad p+r=p+r,
\]
so (1) gives
\[
D_{p+r}=\binom{2(p+r)}{p+r}
\equiv \binom21\binom{2r}{r}=2D_r.
\]
Now suppose \(2r\ge p\). Write \(2r=p+t\), where \(0\le t<p\). Since \(r<p\), we have \(t=2r-p<r\). Thus (1) gives
\[
D_r=\binom{p+t}{r}\equiv\binom10\binom tr=0.
\]
Also
\[
2(p+r)=3p+t,
\]
so another application of (1) gives
\[
D_{p+r}\equiv\binom31\binom tr=0.
\]
Thus (4) holds in this case as well.

We next prove that all the sequence values whose indices lie between \(p\) and \(2p-1\) vanish modulo \(p\). More precisely, for every \(s\) with \(0\le s<p\),
\[
a(p+s)\equiv0,
\qquad c(p+s)\equiv0.
\tag{5}
\]

For \(a(p+s)\), partition the summation indices \(0\le k\le p+s\) into
\[
0\le k\le s,
\qquad s<k<p,
\qquad p\le k\le p+s.
\]
Every term in the middle range is zero modulo \(p\) by (3). Pair the term indexed by \(k\), for \(0\le k\le s\), with the term indexed by \(p+k\). By (2), the fourth powers of their binomial coefficients are congruent. Since \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{p+k}=-(-1)^k.
\]
Consequently the two terms cancel. This proves \(a(p+s)\equiv0\).

The proof for \(c(p+s)\) uses the same partition and pairing. Again, all terms with \(s<k<p\) vanish because the factor \(\binom{p+s}{k}^2\) is zero modulo \(p\). For \(0\le k\le s\), consider the terms indexed by \(k\) and \(p+k\). Their squared factors \(\binom{p+s}{k}^2\) and \(\binom{p+s}{p+k}^2\) are congruent by (2). In the term indexed by \(k\), the product of central binomial factors is
\[
D_kD_{p+s-k}=D_kD_{p+(s-k)}
\equiv D_k\cdot 2D_{s-k}
\tag{6}
\]
by (4). In the term indexed by \(p+k\), that product is
\[
D_{p+k}D_{s-k}
\equiv 2D_kD_{s-k}.
\tag{7}
\]
Thus the non-sign parts of the two terms are equal modulo \(p\), while their signs are opposite because \((-1)^{p+k}=-(-1)^k\). The pair cancels. This proves the second congruence in (5).

It remains to determine the values on the anti-diagonal, namely \(a(p-1)\) and \(c(p-1)\). We use the familiar congruence
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k
\qquad(0\le k<p).
\tag{8}
\]
One direct proof is
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}
=\frac{(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)}{k!}
\equiv\frac{(-1)(-2)\cdots(-k)}{k!}=(-1)^k,
\]
where \(k!\) is invertible modulo \(p\).

Using (8),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4
 =\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are an odd number \(p\) of terms in the last alternating sum, beginning and ending with \(1\), so
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1.
\tag{9}
\]

We now evaluate \(c(p-1)\). Recall that \(p=2m+1\), so \(p-1=2m\). If \(0\le r<p\) and \(2r\ge p\), the argument used above shows
\[
D_r=\binom{2r}{r}\equiv0.
\tag{10}
\]
Consider the summand in \(c(p-1)\) indexed by \(k\). If \(k>m\), then \(2k\ge p\), so \(D_k\equiv0\) by (10). If \(k<m\), put \(r=p-1-k=2m-k\). Then \(m<r<p\), hence \(2r\ge p\), and therefore
\[
D_{p-1-k}=D_r\equiv0.
\]
Thus every summand vanishes modulo \(p\) except the middle summand \(k=m\).

For that middle summand, \(p-1-m=m\) and \(2m=p-1\), so each of the two central binomial factors is \(\binom{p-1}{m}\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
c(p-1)
&\equiv (-1)^m\binom{p-1}{m}^2
                 \binom{2m}{m}^2\\
&=(-1)^m\binom{p-1}{m}^4\\
&\equiv (-1)^m\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^4
 =(-1)^m,
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
where (8) was used in the last line.

We now isolate the determinant argument. Let \(M=(M_{ij})_{0\le i,j\le 2m}\) be any \((2m+1)\times(2m+1)\) matrix over a commutative ring. Suppose
\[
M_{ij}=0\quad\text{whenever }i+j>2m
\tag{12}
\]
and every anti-diagonal entry has the same value \(x\):
\[
M_{i,2m-i}=x\qquad(0\le i\le2m).
\tag{13}
\]
Then
\[
\det M=(-1)^m x^{2m+1}.
\tag{14}
\]
To see this, reverse the order of the rows and call the resulting matrix \(N\), so
\[
N_{ij}=M_{2m-i,j}.
\]
If \(i<j\), then
\[
(2m-i)+j>2m,
\]
so \(N_{ij}=0\) by (12). Hence \(N\) is lower triangular. Its diagonal entries are
\[
N_{ii}=M_{2m-i,i}=x
\]
by (13), and therefore
\[
\det N=x^{2m+1}.
\]
The reversal permutation on \(2m+1\) objects has one inversion for every pair, hence
\[
\binom{2m+1}{2}=m(2m+1)
\]
inversions. Its sign is consequently
\[
(-1)^{m(2m+1)}=(-1)^m,
\]
because \(2m+1\) is odd. Reversing the rows multiplies a determinant by this sign. Since this sign is its own inverse, we obtain (14).

We apply (14) over the field \(\mathbb F_p\), first to
\[
A=(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Here the indices satisfy \(0\le i,j\le p-1=2m\). If \(i+j>2m=p-1\), then \(i+j\ge p\). Write
\[
i+j=p+s.
\]
Because \(i+j\le2p-2\), we have \(0\le s\le p-2<p\). Equation (5) therefore gives
\[
a(i+j)\equiv0.
\]
Thus the entries strictly beyond the anti-diagonal vanish modulo \(p\). On the anti-diagonal, \(i+j=2m=p-1\), and (9) gives the constant value \(x=1\). Formula (14) now yields
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^m1^{2m+1}=(-1)^m
=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.
\]

Finally apply (14) to
\[
C=(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Exactly the same index calculation, now using the second congruence in (5), shows that every entry strictly beyond the anti-diagonal is zero modulo \(p\). By (11), every anti-diagonal entry is
\[
x=c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m.
\]
Consequently
\[
\det C
\equiv (-1)^m\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^{2m+1}.
\]
Since \(2m+1\) is odd, \(\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^{2m+1}=(-1)^m\), and hence
\[
\det C\equiv(-1)^m(-1)^m=(-1)^{2m}=1\pmod p.
\]

This proves both asserted determinant congruences.
